Is a Financial Advisor Worth the Money?

It's the same question as hiring a painter instead of doing it yourself

Ethan Marchand·August 14, 2026·6 min read

Hiring someone to manage your wealth is a lot like hiring a painter to paint your house. Nobody needs a painter — painting a house is not a mystery. Buy the right primer, tape the trim, put on two coats, and most people can get a perfectly good result. The same is true of managing your own money: nothing about a TFSA, an index fund, or a term life policy is secretly unlearnable. Both are genuinely DIY-able. The honest question was never "can I do this myself" — it's whether you actually will, correctly, every year, for the next thirty years.

What painting your own house actually takes

Not just paint and a Saturday. Proper prep work — scraping, sanding, patching, priming — that takes longer than the painting itself and is the part people skip. Knowing which primer stops a stain from bleeding through. Cutting a straight line by hand instead of leaning on tape. Most DIY paint jobs that look "off" don't fail because someone chose the wrong colour — they fail because of the unglamorous prep work nobody budgeted time for.

What DIY investing actually takes

The equivalent "prep work" in personal finance is a lot less visible, and there's more of it than people expect going in.

  • Discipline in a downturn — the plan that looks great on paper has to survive the one week a year it's genuinely tested, when everything you own is down and every instinct says to do something about it.
  • Staying current — contribution limits change every year, capital gains rules get revised, new account types get introduced. None of it is announced loudly, and missing an update can be an expensive way to find out.
  • Coordinating the pieces — your TFSA, RRSP, insurance, and (if you're incorporated) your corporate accounts aren't separate projects. A decision in one almost always has consequences in another, and it's easy to optimize one account while quietly working against yourself in the next.
  • Actually reviewing it — a plan built once at 30 and never revisited isn't really a plan by 50. Life changes; the portfolio and coverage built around the old version of your life usually don't change with it unless someone makes that a standing habit.

Where the analogy stops holding

A bad paint job is obvious the next morning, and it's fixable next weekend. A bad money decision usually isn't obvious for years, and by the time it is, it's often too late to fully undo. Panic-selling during a downturn, letting a policy lapse, missing that a beneficiary designation was never updated after a divorce — these mistakes are quiet. They don't announce themselves the way a streaky wall does. That's really the core difference: painting mistakes are visible and cheap to fix; money mistakes are invisible and compound for decades.

Key takeaway

A lot of an advisor's actual value isn't picking better investments — it's being the person who stops you from making an emotional decision at exactly the worst moment to make one, and who's still checking the plan against your real life five, ten, and twenty years later.

What you're actually paying for

Not a magic ability to pick winning stocks. What you're paying for is time you don't have to spend, technical knowledge that spans tax, insurance, and estate planning at once instead of in isolation, someone accountable for reviewing the plan against a life that keeps changing, and — underrated — the discipline that keeps a plan alive in practice, not just on the page it was written on.

When doing it yourself genuinely makes sense

Plenty of people paint their own homes well, and plenty of people manage their own money well. It tends to come down to the same three things: you have a real, ongoing interest in the subject rather than a one-time burst of motivation; you actually have the time to keep it current, not just set it up once; and you can act calmly with your own money in a genuinely bad year, not just a hypothetical one. If all three are true, DIY is a completely legitimate choice. If one of them usually isn't, that's the gap advice is actually filling.

Either way, it's worth being honest with yourself about which situation you're actually in — not the one you'd like to be in on your best week. If you're not sure which side of that line you're on, that's a reasonable thing to talk through before deciding either way.
